(Wednesday night through next Monday) 
Issued at 239 PM EST Tue Nov 24 2026

On Wednesday night, the mid level low will continue southeastward 
towards the Middle Mississippi River Valley. As it does so, the lobe 
of shortwave energy rotating around its southeastern side will 
continue to push east across the northern Gulf. Guidance is in 
fairly good agreement about the position and movement of the mid 
level closed low, but some uncertainty remains with respect to the 
shortwave. For example, the latest GFS indicates that the wave will 
be deeper and more robust, developing into another closed low 
near coastal Mississippi. Meanwhile, the latest ECMWF solution 
depicts the feature remaining a shallower open wave. In either 
case, southwesterly flow aloft and deep moisture aloft will favor 
numerous to widespread showers in west Georgia spreading east 
overnight, though a deeper shortwave and stronger associated 
surface low will favor heavier rainfall. Cool and stable air under
the lingering high pressure wedge will inhibit the development of
any thunderstorms. In addition to the rain, a tight pressure 
gradient between the wedge and the developing surface low to the 
south will drive strong northeasterly winds on Wednesday night. 
These winds are forecast to range from 15-20 mph with gusts of 
25-30 mph, with stronger gusts of 30-40 mph possible at the 
ridgetops of far north Georgia. As with heavier rain, a stronger 
shortwave and surface low will also favor higher winds.

During the daytime Thursday, the mid level low will continue into 
the Tennessee Valley region while the shortwave and associated 
surface low swing towards the Mid-Atlantic. Trailing showers on the 
back side of the low will come to an end from south to north over 
the course of the morning. A few light showers will remain possible 
in the far northern tier during the afternoon. All told with this 
system, forecast rainfall totals through Thursday are forecast to 
range from 0.75-1.5" in areas north of I-85 and 0.25-0.75" in areas 
to the south. Rainfall amounts are forecast to be lightest in the 
southeastern portions of the forecast area. As alluded to before, 
some uncertainty remains with these totals, with a stronger 
shortwave favoring heavier totals and a weaker shortwave favoring 
lighter totals. The spread of the probabilistic guidance highlights 
this uncertainty, with 90th percentile totals progged as high as 2.5 
inches in north Georgia and 10th percentile totals between 0-0.5 
inches areawide.

The movement of the low up the East Coast is also expected to 
displace the high pressure to the north and weaken the influence of 
the wedge over the forecast area. Winds will shift from northeast to 
northwest on the back side of this low and briefly diminish early 
Thursday morning. NW winds will pick back up through the late 
morning and afternoon, increasing to 15-20 mph with gusts of 25-30 
mph. High temperatures on Thursday will be in the 50s across the 
majority of the area, and low 60s in east-central Georgia. Cool and 
dry air is expected to overspread the Southeast late Thursday into 
Friday. Low temperatures on Friday morning will be noticeably cooler 
than previous days this week, ranging from the mid 20s in the higher 
elevations of far northeast Georgia to the mid 30s in south-central 
Georgia. Model guidance continues to indicate the possibility of 
some wraparound moisture on the southern flank of the mid level low 
and near the Georgia/Tennessee/North Carolina border early Friday 
morning. However, chances of precipitation on Friday morning have 
decreased to less than 10% in this forecast package with the 
movement of the mid level low trending further north.

High temperatures on Friday will range from the upper 40s to low 50s 
in north Georgia (with low to mid 40s in the mountains) and mid 50s 
in central Georgia. Surface high pressure will settle over the 
region on Saturday, leading to another day of benign weather across 
the forecast area. The airmass will begin to moderate under this 
surface high. Lows will be in the upper 20s to mid 30s in north 
Georgia and upper 30s in central Georgia while highs will largely 
climb into the upper 50s to low 60s. As the center of the high moves 
eastward into the Atlantic on Sunday, southerly low level flow will 
promote increasing atmospheric moisture to go along with the 
gradually warming temperatures. A disturbance moving from the Great 
Plains towards the midwest will advance a cold front towards the 
area, which will bring the next chance of rain to the forecast 
Sunday afternoon through Monday morning. However, with ample model 
disagreement with the evolution of the storm system, available 
moisture, and strength of the front, PoPs have been capped at chance 
for that time period.
